task_row_model.query: In a randomized controlled trial with missing outcome data, when is multiple imputation preferable to complete-case analysis, and what assumptions are required for multiple imputation to yield unbiased estimates?

documents.content: Complete-case analysis (available-case analysis) uses only participants with observed outcomes. It is straightforward and can be unbiased if the probability of missingness is independent of both observed and unobserved data (missing completely at random, MCAR). However, MCAR is a strong condition rarely met in practice; if missingness depends on observed covariates, complete-case estimates may be biased. Complete-case also reduces sample size and statistical power. In settings where missingness is related to observed covariates, analytic methods that adjust for those covariates or use weighting can be preferable to discarding incomplete records.

Multiple imputation (MI) is a three-step procedure: create multiple completed datasets by replacing missing values with draws from an imputation model, analyze each dataset with the substantive model, and combine estimates using Rubin's rules to reflect between- and within-imputation uncertainty. MI accommodates uncertainty about missing values and allows standard complete-data methods after imputation. The imputation model should include variables predictive of missingness and of the outcome. MI is often recommended over single imputation methods because it preserves variability and yields valid inferences when its assumptions hold.

Multiple imputation is preferable to complete-case analysis when missingness depends on observed data (missing at random, MAR) rather than being completely unrelated to both observed and unobserved data (MCAR). Under MAR, MI can produce unbiased estimates provided the imputation model is correctly specified and includes the outcome, treatment indicator, and covariates associated with missingness. It must also reflect uncertainty in the imputations and be compatible with the analysis model (congeniality). Practical guidance includes including auxiliary predictors of missingness and using a number of imputations sufficient to capture missing-information variability; results are pooled with Rubin's rules to obtain valid standard errors.

Nonresponse in survey research is frequently addressed by weighting adjustments and calibration rather than by imputing missing item values. Survey weights can be adjusted so respondents with similar auxiliary characteristics represent nonrespondents, reducing bias when nonresponse correlates with those auxiliaries. Hot-deck imputation copies observed values from similar respondents and is sometimes used for categorical survey items. These approaches focus on population estimates under complex sampling designs and incorporate design weights and clustering; they address different practical concerns than model-based methods intended for causal inference in randomized experiments.

Discussion of intention-to-treat (ITT) versus per-protocol analysis centers on preserving randomization and handling protocol deviations. ITT analyzes participants according to assigned treatment regardless of adherence, guarding against selection bias from post-randomization exclusions. Per-protocol and as-treated analyses can estimate treatment efficacy under full adherence but are vulnerable to confounding when nonadherence is informative. Methods such as instrumental variables or complier average causal effects are used to estimate causal effects in the presence of noncompliance; these are distinct issues from techniques for handling missing outcome data.
